To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

heme A synthases in bacteria depend on one pair of extracytoplasmically exposed cysteinyls that form disulfide bonds for activity and that the cysteine pair is not required for heme O binding but is essential for the oxygen-dependent heme A synthesis.
the essential cysteinyl residues of heme A synthesases mediate the transfer of reducing equivalents for the synthesis of hemes A from heme Os.
the essential pair of cysteines in heme A synthases from bacteria and archaea is required for catalysis and that the pair of cystein residues can form a disulfide bridge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanism of heme A biosynthesis, an essential step in the assembly of the respiratory oxidases of mitochondria, bacteria and archaea.
the structure and mechanism of a heme A synthetase, a poorly understood membrane enzyme that catalyzes the biosynthesis of the unique heme A prosthetic group of cytochrome oxidase.
the structure-function relationship of heme A biosynthetic enzymes in bacteria and mitochondria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cysteines are essential for the catalysis of the heme O to heme A reaction.

heme A synthases from bacteria, mitochondria and plants all contain one or two pairs cysteine residues and that the cysteinyls in the bacterial enzymes are essential for the catalysis of hemes A formation.
the two cysteines in loop I/II of heme A syntheses are essential for the catalysis of hemesynthesis, but are not essential for binding of the heme O substrate to the enzyme protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the heme A synthases from bacteria and mitochondria are functionally and mechanistically distinct.
the heme A synthases of eubacteria and archaea have a common catalytic mechanism but that the eubacteria have evolved an extra pair of cysteinys that are not present in the archaea.
heme A synthases are membrane-anchored proteins with a hydrophilic loop containing a disulfide bridge and that the disulfide bridge is required for catalysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
heme A synthases are not all created equal and that the enzyme from B. subtils and A. perniz is the most similar to the mitochondrial enzyme.
heme A synthases in bacteria, mitochondria and plants have a similar catalytic mechanism.
heme A synthases from bacteria are not only different from those of mitochondria, but also differ from each other.
